Gruvlok grooved mechanical fittings and couplings for fire protection, HVAC and industrial piping. Sizes 2" through 12", in painted carbon steel, galvanized, 304 and 316 stainless.

A grooved joint is made by rolling or cutting a groove near the pipe end, seating a gasket over the gap and bolting a two-piece housing around it. It goes together far faster than welding or flanging on large diameters, needs no hot work permit, and can be taken apart for service — which is why it dominates riser and mechanical-room piping.

Rigid and flexible couplings are not the same product. Flexible couplings allow angular deflection and absorb thermal movement and vibration; rigid couplings do not and are required where the system must behave as a solid assembly. Mixing them incorrectly shows up as noise and stressed joints.

Gasket compound must match the medium and temperature. EPDM (green) is the standard for water and is not suitable for petroleum service.

Black malleable iron threaded fittings for gas, steam, compressed air and hydronic heating. Sizes 1/8" through 4", in FIP, MPT x FPT, three-way FPT and flanged configurations.

Black iron is used on gas because it carries no zinc. Zinc coating can shed inside a fuel gas line and the flakes foul controls and orifices downstream, which is why black is the trade default even though a galvanized fitting looks identical on the shelf. NFPA 54 does permit galvanized steel pipe for fuel gas, so the requirement on any given job comes from the local code and the gas utility rather than from a blanket ban.

Threads are NPT and taper — the seal comes from thread deformation, not from the sealant, so the correct engagement depth matters more than how much dope is applied. Use a sealant rated for the medium: standard pipe dope is not approved for gas, where a yellow gas-rated PTFE tape or a listed compound is required.

Galvanized malleable iron fittings in 1/8" through 4", threaded NPT. Tees, couplings, bushings, 90° elbows, street and adapter elbows, and plugs, in FIP, MPT x FPT, three-way FPT and flanged patterns.

These are the same malleable iron castings used in black iron, finished with a hot-dip zinc coating. That coating is the whole difference: it buys external corrosion resistance for damp, exposed and outdoor runs, at the cost of internal flaking over long service life.

Do not use galvanized on interior fuel gas. Zinc shed from the coating travels downstream and fouls regulators, valves and burner orifices, and most codes prohibit it outright — black iron is the material for gas.

Where galvanized meets copper, install a dielectric union. The two metals in contact with water between them form a galvanic cell, and the steel side corrodes through at the joint well before either pipe reaches its normal service life.

Brass is chosen over steel here for corrosion resistance and machinability rather than strength, and over plastic where the joint has to be taken apart repeatedly or exposed to heat. Dezincification is the failure mode to design against. In acidic or high-chloride water, zinc leaches out of ordinary brass over years and leaves a porous copper structure that eventually fails under pressure. DZR (dezincification-resistant) alloy solves it and is worth specifying where local water is known to be aggressive.

ABS joins with a one-step solvent cement — no primer, unlike PVC — which makes it faster in cold conditions and is part of why it remains standard in much of the western U.S. and Canada. The cement is not interchangeable with PVC cement, and transition cement is required where the two materials meet.

Sanitary tees, wyes, tee-wye combinations, double configurations and closet flanges make up most of the range. The distinction between a sanitary tee and a wye matters at inspection: a sanitary tee is only permitted where flow changes from horizontal to vertical, never from vertical to horizontal, where a long-sweep wye is required.

Frequently asked questions

What does a backwater valve do?

A backwater valve lets wastewater flow out of the building but closes if the sewer backs up, so sewage cannot come back in through floor drains and low fixtures. Match the valve to the pipe size and material, such as 2" ABS.

Why support an expansion tank with a bracket?

A thermal expansion tank full of water is heavy, and hanging it from the water heater piping puts that weight on the fittings. A bracket such as the Sioux Chief 598-023 carries the tank so the piping does not have to.

F1807 crimp or F1960 expansion PEX fittings?

They are different systems with different tools. F1807 fittings are crimped with a copper or stainless ring; F1960 fittings need expansion PEX tubing and an expansion tool. Match the fitting to the system already installed. See F1807 crimp fittings.

Frequently asked questions

Which TOTO flapper do I need?

Match the flapper to the flush valve in the tank. Many TOTO tanks use a 3" flush valve, which takes flappers such as the THU500S, and some older models use a 2" valve. Check the tank model number, printed inside the tank.

Will a TOTO fill valve fit any toilet?

The TSU99A.XR is an adjustable fill valve made for TOTO tanks. Set its height to the tank as described in the instructions, so the water level sits at the mark inside the tank.

Elongated or round TOTO seat?

Measure from the seat bolt holes to the front edge of the bowl: about 18-1/2" is elongated and about 16-1/2" is round. TOTO SoftClose seats are made in both shapes.

Frequently asked questions

What do I need to install a wall-mount toilet?

An in-wall carrier and concealed tank made for that bowl, plus the actuator plate and seat if they are not included. Confirm the carrier system before ordering the bowl.

Can the bowl height be adjusted?

Yes. On a wall-hung toilet the carrier sets the bowl height, which is how ADA rim heights are reached.

Do wall-mount toilets save space?

They free up floor space and make cleaning under the bowl easy, while the tank sits inside the wall cavity.

One hundred six toilet bowls sold separately from the tank, for two-piece installations, wall-hung carriers and commercial flushometer applications. From American Standard (46), TOTO (36), Gerber (20), Duravit (2) and DXV (2), $97 to $809. The matching toilet tanks are on their own page.

Elongated or round front

An elongated toilet bowl runs about two inches longer front to back and is the more comfortable of the two, which is why 83 of the bowls here are elongated. Round front - 16 of them - buys those two inches back, and that matters more often than people expect: a door that swings into the fixture, a vanity opposite, a powder room where the code clearance in front of the bowl is already tight. Measure the space in front of the flange before you decide on comfort.

Chair height, comfort height and right height are the same thing

Three names, one specification. All of them mean a bowl whose rim sits roughly 16-1/2 to 18 inches off the floor instead of the traditional 14-1/2 to 15. Twenty-four bowls here are called out as chair or right height. Standing up off one is easier on knees and hips, which is the whole point - and it is also why it has quietly become the default in new residential work.

One measurement detail people get wrong: the height that matters is to the top of the seat, not the rim. A seat adds roughly half an inch to an inch, so a 17-inch rim and a thick seat can land above the range you were aiming for.

What ADA actually requires

Thirteen bowls here are specifically called out as ADA, including American Standard's Afwall ADA Retrofit. It is worth being precise about what that means, because the bowl is only one input. The standard asks for a seat top between 17 and 19 inches, clear floor space beside and in front of the fixture, a flush control on the open side of the approach, and an operating force that a closed fist can manage. A chair height bowl makes compliance possible; the installation, the seat and the flush control decide whether you get there. If you are specifying for a commercial job, work from the drawing, not from the product page.

Rough-in: check it, and know where to find it

Rough-in is the distance from the finished wall to the centreline of the closet bolts. Twelve inches is standard; 10" and 14" exist in older construction, and a bowl for the wrong rough-in will not sit against the wall.

Being straight about a gap in our own listings: only one of these 106 states the rough-in in the title. Work from the model number, or from the manufacturer's spec sheet for that model. And if the flange is in the wrong place and moving the drain is not realistic, the TOTO Unifit adapters convert a single bowl between 10", 12" and 14" - that is exactly the problem they exist to solve.

Three different machines: tank-type, wall-hung and flushometer

Eighty-nine of these are conventional tank-type bowls for a two-piece toilet. Ten are wall-hung, which carry no weight on the floor and need a carrier inside the wall - the Geberit and Grohe in-wall carriers are with the toilet repair parts. Seven are floor-mount flushometer bowls with no tank connection at all: they take a spud and a flush valve fed straight off the supply, which is why you see them in schools and offices where a tank could not refill fast enough between uses.

Thirteen bowls carry a spud - ten top spud, three back spud - and the two are not interchangeable. Top spud takes the flush valve above the bowl; back spud takes it behind, through the wall. Match it to the valve and the wall penetration you already have.

Skirted bowls and EverClean

Ten of these are skirted: the trapway is concealed behind a smooth outer wall instead of the usual moulded contour. The reason is cleaning - there is no channel behind the bowl to reach into. The trade-off is that skirted bowls usually mount with a bracket system rather than plain closet bolts, so read the install instructions before you assume it drops onto the existing flange. Thirteen bowls carry American Standard's EverClean glaze, and seven ship with a seat included.

Match the bowl to the tank

Four of these are pressure assist bowls, which only work with a pressure assist tank - the vessel is in the tank, and the bowl's trapway is sized for that discharge. The same logic holds more generally: flush volume, trapway and tank outlet are engineered as a set. Buy the bowl and the tank from the same model family, and if you are replacing only one half, match the model number on the piece you are keeping.

Seventy-eight toilet tanks sold on their own, without a bowl, from American Standard (34), TOTO (20), Gerber (18), Duravit (4) and DXV (2). Prices run from $60 to $795. If you need the other half, the toilet bowls are on their own page.

A toilet tank is not a universal part

This is the one thing worth getting right before anything else. A two-piece toilet is engineered as a matched pair: the tank's outlet, its bolt pattern, its flush valve height and its water volume are all designed around one specific bowl. A replacement toilet tank from the correct model family will bolt down and flush properly. One that merely looks similar will either not seat on the bolt holes, or will seat and then flush badly forever. Find the model number cast inside your existing tank - usually on the back wall above the water line, or under the lid - and match it.

Rough-in: 10, 12 or 14 inches

Rough-in is the distance from the finished wall to the centre of the closet flange bolts. Twelve inches is the modern standard and covers 36 of the tanks here; 6 are built for a 10-inch rough-in, common in houses built before the 1960s and in some compact bathrooms, and one is 14-inch. The Duravit DuraSystem WD1022000091 is different again - an in-wall carrier tank that hides inside a 2x4 or 2x6 stud bay.

Forty-four of these carry the rough-in in the product title. For the other 34 - most of the TOTO range among them - check the specification block further down the product page, where it often appears. Where it is not listed at all, work from the bowl's model number rather than from a tape measure, because the manufacturer pairs the tank to a named bowl rather than to a dimension.

Flush volume has to match the bowl

Forty-eight of these are 1.28 gpf, the current federal maximum for a new toilet; 15 are 1.6 gpf for older bowls designed around that volume; a handful are 1.0 and 1.1 gpf high-efficiency. Putting a 1.28 gpf tank on a bowl engineered for 1.6 gpf does not save water - it starves a trapway sized for more, and you get double flushes, which uses more. Match what the bowl was built for.

Dual flush and pressure assist

Eight tanks are dual flush: a full flush for solids and a reduced one for liquids, either through a split trip lever or a top push button. The TOTO Aquia IV family and Duravit's DuraStyle and ME by Starck use the button.

Four American Standard tanks are pressure assist, and these are a different machine entirely. Inside the china tank sits a sealed plastic vessel. Incoming line pressure compresses air above the water, and the flush releases that stored pressure rather than relying on gravity and head height. The result is a forceful, short, loud flush that clears a bowl in one go - which is why they are standard in commercial restrooms. None of the internal parts interchange with a gravity tank, and they need a minimum of about 20 psi of static line pressure to work.

Trip lever hand and WASHLET+ routing

Thirteen of these have a right-hand trip lever and five are explicitly left-hand; the rest are standard left. It sounds trivial until the toilet sits in a corner or beside a vanity and the handle is against the wall. Separately, twelve TOTO tanks are WASHLET+ compatible, which means the tank is built to route the supply line to a bidet seat through a concealed connection rather than a visible tee - a detail that only matters if you are installing a WASHLET, and matters a lot if you are.

Lined tanks and colours

American Standard's "Lined" tanks (4188A054, 4188A154 and 4425A154) carry a foam liner bonded to the inside of the china. In a humid bathroom, cold supply water chills the tank wall below the dew point and it sweats - the puddle on the floor that looks like a leak but is not. The liner stops it. Ten tanks here come in something other than plain white: Bone, Linen, Sedona Beige, Colonial White, Canvas White and Ebony.

What else the job needs

A tank swap is rarely just the tank. You will want the tank-to-bowl gasket and bolt set, and a new flush valve and fill valve if the old ones are anything but new - see toilet repair parts. If the toilet is coming off the floor, add a wax ring and closet bolts. And while the water is off, it is the right moment to replace the angle stop and the toilet supply line, which together cost less than the trip back.

65 toilet seats from Toto (26), Bemis (16), Duravit (10), American Standard (9) and DXV (4) — round and elongated, closed front and open front, in plastic, enameled wood and electronic bidet.

Round or elongated is the first thing to get right, and it is measured on the bowl, not the seat. Take the distance from the centre of the two bolt holes at the back to the outside front edge of the china. Round comes out around 16-1/2"; elongated around 18-1/2". The seats stocked here bear that out — the round ones run 16-5/16" to 16-7/8" front to back and the elongated run 18-7/16" to 19-1/16". A seat one size off will bolt down and still overhang or undercut the rim, and it is the single most common reason a seat goes back in the box.

Open front is a code requirement, not a style. Public and employee restrooms generally call for an open-front seat, with or without a cover depending on the occupancy — the split in the bowl-front is there so the seat is not contacted where it matters. 13 open-front seats are stocked, from Toto, Bemis and American Standard, most of them heavy duty for commercial traffic. A closed-front residential seat in a public restroom is a failed inspection, and the local code is what settles which version applies.

The hinge is what wears out, not the seat. Bemis names the mechanism in the model: a self-sustaining check hinge holds the seat and lid wherever they are left, which is what a commercial spec usually calls for; a non-self-sustaining hinge lets them fall. STA-TITE and Top-Tite are the mounting systems — they clamp the seat so it stops shifting side to side, which is the failure that makes a good seat feel cheap after a year. Where the seat has to come off for cleaning, the telescoping and lift-off models release without tools.

32 of these are soft-close or slow-close: the lid and ring drop under damping instead of slamming, which saves the hinge, the china and the household. Toto calls it SoftClose, Duravit and American Standard call it slow-close, and the mechanism does the same job.

Material splits three ways. Plastic — polypropylene on most of these — is light, easy to sanitize and the standard for commercial. Enameled wood is heavier and warmer to sit on, and three are stocked in that construction from Bemis. Toto’s EverClean and comparable surfaces add a glaze that resists staining on high-traffic bowls.

Electronic bidet seats are the other category here entirely. Nine are stocked — Toto WASHLET (S7A, S7, K300, A2 and a WASHLET+ Ready square), the DXV AT100 SpaLet and two Duravit SensoWash, one of them with remote and app control. All of them need power at the toilet, which means a GFCI receptacle within reach of the cord and usually an electrician before the plumber. The WASHLET+ models are built to pair with specific Toto bowls that route the supply and cord out of sight — check the bowl before ordering the seat, because the concealed connection only works on the matched pairing.

Related: toilet bowls, toilet repair parts, flush valve parts, wax rings and bolts, connected home equipment and the full bathroom range.

Frequently asked questions

How do I know if I need a round or elongated seat?

Measure the bowl from the center of the two bolt holes to the front edge of the rim. About 16-1/2" is round and about 18-1/2" is elongated.

Do electronic bidet seats need an outlet?

Yes. They need power at the toilet, usually a GFCI receptacle within reach of the cord, and a water connection at the toilet supply.

What is the difference between open-front and closed-front seats?

Open-front seats have a gap at the front and are common in public and commercial restrooms, where codes often require them. Closed-front seats are the usual residential style.

One hundred twenty-nine toilet repair parts: fill valves, flappers, flush valves, trip levers and push-button actuators, tank-to-bowl kits and gaskets, rough-in adapters, flange spacers and shims. From TOTO (43), Fluidmaster (29), Pasco (11), Sioux Chief (9), American Standard (8), Duravit (7), Geberit (7), Oatey (4), DXV (4), Moen (3), Brizo (2) and Grohe (2).

Which part do I need?

  • Toilet runs or refills by itself: replace the flapper. Measure the opening in the tank bottom first, 2" or 3".
  • Tank fills slowly, overfills or hisses: replace the fill valve. Universal fill valves fit most two-piece toilets.
  • New flapper still leaks: the flush valve seat is worn. Replace the flush valve or use a seat repair kit.
  • Handle is loose or will not lift the flapper: replace the trip lever (front, left or right mount).
  • Water drips between the tank and bowl: fit a tank-to-bowl kit made for your toilet brand.
  • Leak or rocking at the floor: replace the wax ring and closet bolts, see wax rings and bolts.
  • Commercial toilet with a flushometer (no tank): see flush valve parts and repair kits or a new toilet flush valve.

A cracked tank or bowl cannot be repaired with parts: see replacement toilet tanks, toilet bowls or complete toilets.

Diagnose it before you buy

Almost every toilet complaint is one of two parts. A toilet that runs - water trickling into the bowl, the tank refilling every few minutes with nobody in the room - is nearly always the flapper. A toilet that refills slowly, overfills into the overflow tube, or hammers when it shuts off is nearly always the fill valve. They age together, so replacing both at once costs little more than one part and saves the second trip.

Flapper size is the first thing to check

Two-inch and three-inch flush valves are both common, they look identical in a photograph, and a 2" toilet flapper on a 3" valve will not seal at all. Measure the opening in the bottom of the tank before ordering - not the flapper you pulled out, which may itself have been the wrong part.

Fluidmaster's PRO53, PRO54 and PRO55 are universal-fit flappers; the PRO56 and the 502P21 Adjust-A-Flush are adjustable, which lets you tune how long the flapper stays open and therefore how much water each flush uses. The PRO58 is the 3" adjustable. Pasco's 22001 and 22054 are the plain 2" trade flappers. TOTO's THU500S fits their 3" tanks, and the THU227 is the Aquia dual-flush seal, sold ten to a pack.

One thing that kills flappers: in-tank chlorine tablets. The rubber goes hard and glazed in months instead of years. If the flapper you removed feels like a hockey puck, that is why.

Fill valves

The Fluidmaster 400A is the part most American toilets end up with eventually - a universal anti-siphon toilet fill valve that adjusts for height. The 400LS adds Leak Sentry, which shuts the valve if the flapper leaks. The PRO45, PRO45B and PRO45K are the contractor-grade versions, and the K is the kit with the shank washer and refill tube. American Standard's 7381125-400 and TOTO's TSU99A.XR are the manufacturer equivalents. TOTO's Geberit-style concealed tanks take their own filling-valve nipple and fixation clip.

Set the water level to the mark moulded into the overflow tube - usually about an inch below its top. Higher and the tank simply drains into the overflow forever; lower and the flush is weak.

Flush valve is not the same as the flapper

The flapper is the rubber seal. The flush valve is the whole seat-and-overflow assembly it sits on, and it only needs replacing when the seat itself is pitted or cracked - run a fingertip around it, and if it catches, no new flapper will seal. Fluidmaster's 507AP7, PRO57 and PRO57K cover the common sizes; the 555CRP8 Flusher Fixer Kit bonds a new seat over the old one without pulling the tank, which is the repair to reach for when the tank bolts are corroded.

Trip levers are handed, and the nut is reverse-threaded

Front, left-side and right-side mount are separate parts - check which one you have before ordering. And the trip lever nut is left-hand threaded on most brands: it tightens counterclockwise. This catches people constantly, because the instinct when it will not loosen is to pull harder in the direction that is actually tightening it.

Levers are visible, so finish matters: chrome, brushed nickel, polished nickel, matte black, platinum, cotton white and ebony are all stocked. TOTO's THU068 fits Drake tanks except the R-suffix models, which is the kind of detail worth reading twice. For in-wall tanks, six TOTO DuoFit push-button plates and the Duravit, Geberit, Grohe and DXV actuator plates replace the lever entirely.

Tank-to-bowl kits are brand-specific

The bolts, washers and sponge gasket between tank and bowl are not universal - the bolt spacing and the gasket diameter follow the manufacturer. Sioux Chief stocks six kits by brand: American Standard, Gerber, Kohler (two versions), Eljer and Mansfield. American Standard has its own EZ Install kits, and TOTO's gaskets are called out per toilet model rather than per size. If you are pulling a tank, replace the gasket and bolts - they are a few dollars and they are the reason the tank leaks at the base.

Unifit adapters change a toilet's rough-in

Seven TOTO Unifit trapway adapters let one bowl serve a 10", 12" or 14" rough-in. This is genuinely useful in a remodel where the flange is not where the new toilet expects it: instead of moving the drain, you fit the matching adapter. TSU01W covers CT474, MS614 and MS644; TSU03W the 934, 964 and 974 one-piece toilets; TSU08W the Aquia IV. See replacement toilet tanks for the rough-in question from the tank side.

Flange spacers, shims and Liquilock

When the finished floor went in over the old one, the closet flange ends up below the tile and the bowl rocks. Oatey's 43412 and 43413 flange spacers (1/4" and 1/8") and the Pasco 1018 extension bring it back up; Sioux Chief's Wedge-It shims level the bowl without shimming with coins. And Oatey Liquilock is the one nobody knows about - a gel that turns the water in the bowl and trap solid so you can lift the toilet without it running down the hallway. It liquefies again with water.

Frequently asked questions

Why does my toilet keep running?

A running toilet is almost always the flapper or the fill valve. Put a few drops of food coloring in the tank: if color reaches the bowl without flushing, the flapper or flush valve seal is leaking. If the water level rises into the overflow tube, the fill valve needs adjusting or replacing.

Do I need a 2-inch or 3-inch flapper?

Match the flush valve opening in the tank. Many older toilets use 2-inch valves and many newer high-efficiency toilets use 3-inch valves, so check the toilet model or measure the drain opening.

Are toilet repair parts universal?

Many fill valves are universal, but flush valves, flappers, canister seals and tank-to-bowl gaskets for brands like TOTO and American Standard are often model-specific. Match the part to the toilet model number printed inside the tank.

Material sets the feel and the install. Escutcheons, floor and ceiling plates: the trim rings that cover the opening where pipe passes through a wall, floor or ceiling.

Depth is the specification that decides whether one works. A shallow escutcheon sits nearly flat and covers a neat hole; a deep flange escutcheon has a raised skirt and covers a ragged or oversized opening that a shallow one leaves visible. On a retrofit, measure the actual opening before ordering — this is the single most common return in the category.

Sizing follows the pipe, and the pipe standard matters: CTS (copper tube size) and IPS (iron pipe size) escutcheons of the same nominal number have different bores and are not interchangeable.

Split (hinged) versions exist for pipe already installed, so the trim can go on without breaking a joint.

Floor and ceiling plates do the same job on vertical risers, and in a fire-rated assembly the escutcheon is cosmetic only — the penetration still needs a listed firestop behind it.

Brands include Pasco, Sioux Chief, Dearborn and Delta.

What is the difference between widespread and centerset?

A widespread faucet has a separate spout and two handles, usually 8 inches apart. A centerset puts the spout and handles on one base over 4-inch holes.

Do Moen widespread trim kits include the valve?

Are the handles included?

Can a single-hole faucet go on a three-hole sink?

What is a vessel faucet?

Fifty-one centerset bathroom faucets from Moen (20), Delta (8), American Standard (7), Gerber (7), Matco-Norca (6), Elkay, Grohe and Zurn. Thirty-three are two-handle, seventeen single-handle, and one is a cover plate. $28 to $536.

What centerset means, and how to know you need one

A 4-inch centerset faucet fits a sink with three holes drilled 4 inches apart, centre to centre, measured between the two outer holes. The spout and both handles sit on one continuous base plate that covers all three. It is the most common configuration in American bathrooms and it is what almost every builder-grade vanity top is drilled for.

The two alternatives: a single-hole faucet needs one hole and one only, and a widespread faucet uses three holes spread 8 to 16 inches apart with the spout and handles as separate pieces. Count the holes and measure between the outer two before ordering - it is the one measurement that decides everything, and it takes ten seconds.

What people get wrong: the 4 inches is not the width of the faucet, and it is not the distance between the handles you can see. It is hole to hole in the deck.

Single-handle on a centerset deck

Seventeen of these are single-handle faucets built on a 4" base plate - one lever, but still covering the three-hole drilling. Delta's Classic (501-DST, 520-MPU-DST) and Foundations (B501LF, B510LF), Moen's Chateau L64621, American Standard's Colony PRO 7075000 and Reliant 3. This is the answer when you want the look of one handle without redrilling or replacing the vanity top.

Commercial, institutional and ADA handles

Eight faucets here are built for public and institutional restrooms: Moen's M-DURA (8215F12, 8413F12) and M-BITION 8915, Delta's Commercial HDF 501LF-HDF, Zurn's AquaSpec Z81104-XL-3M with a vandal-resistant pressure-compensating aerator, Elkay's LK402T4, and American Standard's Monterrey 5500170 and 7500180.

The giveaway is the handle. Wrist blade and long lever handles exist because the accessibility standard requires a faucet that can be operated without tight grasping, pinching or twisting of the wrist, with no more than five pounds of force. A round knob fails that on its face; a four-inch wrist blade passes, because a forearm or a closed fist will turn it. If you are specifying for a school, clinic or public building, that is the detail the inspector looks at.

Flow rate

Four faucets here run 0.5 gpm, which is the public-restroom standard - low enough that a running tap wastes very little, and paired with laminar flow on the American Standard Monterrey 7500180 so the stream does not aerosolise. Eight run 1.2 gpm, now the common residential specification and below the WaterSense threshold. Three run 1.5 gpm, the federal maximum for a lavatory faucet. For a home bathroom, 1.2 gpm is the sensible default; 0.5 gpm in a residence will feel starved.

Check whether the drain is included

Twelve of these ship with a drain assembly - Gerber's touch-down and 50/50 pop-up drains, Moen's metal pop-up on the Brantford and Gibson. The rest do not. That is worth ten or twenty dollars and a second order, so compare on the whole package rather than the faucet price. The Gerber DA667229BN cover plate is the other side of the same question: it lets a single-hole faucet sit on a three-hole sink, which is how you go the other direction without a new top.

84 kitchen faucets — 64 pull-down and 20 pull-out — from Moen (23), Delta (14), Gerber (14), Grohe (11), Hansgrohe (8), Brizo, Matco-Norca, Franke, Peerless, American Standard, Elkay and Rohl. All single handle, 1.5 or 1.75 gpm, in polished chrome, stainless, matte black, oil rubbed bronze, champagne bronze, brushed gold and graphite.

Pull-down or pull-out is decided by the sink and the wall behind it, not by the faucet. A pull-down has a tall arc and the sprayer comes straight down into the bowl — it wants headroom, and it is the right answer over a deep single-bowl sink. A pull-out has a lower spout and the sprayer comes toward you, which is what works under a window, beneath a low upper cabinet, or on a shallow or double-bowl sink where a high arc would just splash. The pull-out also reaches further onto the counter, which matters if you fill pots off the sink rather than in it. Measure the clearance from the deck to whatever is above it before choosing the arc.

The retraction system is the part that fails, and every brand solves it differently. Moen's Reflex and Gerber's SnapBack both use a counterweight on the hose to pull the sprayer back and hold it docked; Moen's Power Clean and Power Boost are spray-force features, not docking ones. When a sprayer sags out of the spout or will not seat, the cause is almost always under the sink and not in the head: the counterweight has slid along the hose, or the hose is snagged on a shutoff, a disposal or the trap. Reseat the weight at the manufacturer's spacing and clear the hose path before replacing anything.

A single-handle faucet needs one hole, and most sinks are drilled for three. That gap is what the deck plate covers, and it is the part people leave off the order and then discover on installation day. Some faucets here ship with one — Gerber's G0040164 Viper names it in the box — and for the rest it is a separate line item. Check the sink's hole count and spacing before ordering, because a three-hole sink with a one-hole faucet and no deck plate cannot be finished.

Flow is capped by law: the federal maximum for a kitchen faucet is 2.2 gpm, and several states set a lower limit. Nothing here exceeds 1.75 gpm and the Grohe Concetto and several Delta and American Standard models run 1.5, so the stock clears the stricter state caps as well as the federal one.

Five brands, five names for the same silver finish. Moen calls it Spot Resist Stainless, Delta calls it Arctic Stainless, Grohe calls it SuperSteel, Hansgrohe calls it Stainless Steel Optic and Franke calls it Stainless Steel. They photograph almost identically and they do not match each other across a kitchen. If the sink, the faucet and the disposal air switch come from three brands, pick the finish family once and accept that only one of them will be exact.

Spray patterns run from a single stream to dual and triple spray, and spout reach from a 14" prep faucet to a 17.5" high-arc. Bar and prep sinks have their own shorter line in pull-out prep and bar faucets; replacement sprayers and hoses are in faucet parts.

Trim is bought separately from the valve body and only fits the valve family it was designed for. A Moen trim will not fit a Delta rough-in, and within a brand the cartridge generation matters — a trim for a current valve often will not seat on a fifteen-year-old body even though the brand matches. Identify the valve before ordering the trim.

The most common retrofit surprise is escutcheon coverage. A new trim with a smaller plate exposes the ring of unfinished tile the old one hid, which turns a trim swap into a tile repair.

Finishes stocked here are chrome, matte black, brushed nickel, stainless and oil-rubbed bronze. Oil-rubbed bronze is a living finish on some lines and changes with handling, so pieces bought years apart may not match.

Brands include Moen, Delta, Pfister and Gerber.

Frequently asked questions

What comes in a tub and shower trim kit?

Usually the handle, the escutcheon plate, the tub spout and the showerhead. Kits marked "no head" or "NH" leave out the showerhead, and every kit leaves out the rough-in valve.

How do I know which trim kit fits my valve?

Match the brand and valve family. For Moen, a Posi-Temp valve takes Posi-Temp trim and an M-CORE valve takes M-CORE trim of the same series.

What is the difference between a tub/shower trim and a shower-only trim?

A tub/shower kit includes a tub spout with a diverter. A shower-only kit has just the handle, escutcheon and showerhead.

Finish naming is not standardized between manufacturers. Does a shower trim kit include the valve?

No. A trim kit is the handle, escutcheon and showerhead. The rough-in valve in the wall is sold separately, and the trim must match its brand and valve family.

What does "shower only" mean on a Moen trim?

It means the kit has no tub spout. It is for a stand-up shower; for a tub and shower combination, see tub-shower trim sets.

Can I replace only the shower handle?

Yes. If the showerhead is staying, a valve-only trim with just the handle and escutcheon is the simpler part.

Shower and tub-shower rough-in valves: the valve body that goes in the wall before it closes, in pressure-balance, thermostatic and multi-outlet configurations.

The rough-in and the finish trim are two separate purchases, and that is deliberate — the valve can be set during construction and the finish chosen months later. It also means the two must belong to the same manufacturer family. A Moen trim will not fit a Delta body, and cartridge families change between generations within a single brand.

Pressure-balance is the code minimum in most jurisdictions: it holds the hot-cold ratio when pressure drops elsewhere, which stops the scald when a toilet flushes. Thermostatic holds the actual outlet temperature and lets you set a number, which is what a multi-outlet shower needs.

Check whether the body includes integral stops. Without them, servicing the cartridge means shutting off the whole house.

Brands include Moen, Delta, Grohe and Brizo.

Shower valve replacement

If a shower drips, runs too hot or too cold, or the handle is stiff, the fix is usually the cartridge, not the whole valve. Replace the valve body when it is corroded, leaking inside the wall, or not pressure-balanced. Staying with the same brand and valve family keeps your trim options open and can limit how much tile you need to open. Find cartridges in tub and shower repair parts, and match the finish with shower trim sets, tub-shower trim sets or thermostatic valve trims.

Frequently asked questions

What is a rough-in shower valve?

It is the valve body that is plumbed into the wall before the tile goes up. The handle and escutcheon (the trim) are bought separately and mount over it.

Pressure-balance or thermostatic: which do I need?

Pressure-balance valves keep the hot and cold mix steady when pressure changes and meet code in most homes. Thermostatic valves hold a set temperature and are the usual choice for showers with several outlets.

Which connection type should I choose?

Pick the inlet that matches your supply pipe: sweat (CC) for copper, IPS for threaded pipe, or crimp ring or cold-expansion PEX. Many Moen M-PACT and M-CORE valves are listed by connection type in the title.

Which Moen valve do I have?

Is the valve included with Moen trim kits?

What does Posi-Temp mean?

Posi-Temp is Moen's pressure-balancing valve. It keeps the hot and cold mix steady when water pressure changes elsewhere in the house, such as when a toilet flushes.

Can I change the finish of my shower without opening the wall?

Yes, if the new trim is made for the valve that is already installed. Swapping trim on the same valve family is done from the finished wall.

How do I find American Standard toilet parts for my toilet?

A water heater is the appliance most likely to flood a house, and the one most often installed where nobody looks. These are automatic shut-off valves that sit on the cold supply to the heater and close it when a sensor finds water on the floor or in the pan. Orders ship from Seattle, WA.

Taco LEAKBREAKER is a control unit with a motorized 3/4 in. NPT ball valve, actuator and floor sensor, built specifically for a water heater. It is resettable and testable after a trip, so a nuisance alarm does not mean a service call, and it signals with a two-color LED and an audible alarm. The LB-075-H-1LF ships with one sensor, the LB-075-H-2LF with two, for a heater with both a pan and a nearby floor drain. The eLink version (LBW-075-H-2LF) adds WiFi and reports status and trips to your phone.

FloodStop 20001 is the same idea at a lower price point: a 3/4 in. NPT MIP x FIP valve with control unit and sensor. The MIP x FIP body threads inline with the existing supply nipple, so the install is a union break rather than a pipe cut.

Sizing and placement. All four are 3/4 in. NPT, which is the supply on effectively every residential tank heater. Put the valve on the cold inlet, upstream of the heater, and the sensor at the low point of the pan or the floor. A shut-off on the heater protects the heater only — if you want the whole house covered, a main-line valve is the right device.

70 water pressure regulators and service parts, 1/2" through 2": Resideo DS05 and DS06 DialSet (32, including six repair parts), Watts 009 series (13), Cash Acme EB45 and F95 (10), Zurn Wilkins 600XL, 70XL and NR3XL (8), Caleffi North America PressCal (6) and one Apollo-Conbraco direct acting valve. The trade calls the device a PRV and the fixture aisle calls it a water pressure regulator; they are the same valve.

A pressure reducing valve and a pressure relief valve do opposite jobs. A regulator sits on the incoming service and holds downstream pressure at a set point continuously, whether or not anything is wrong. A relief valve does nothing at all until pressure or temperature crosses a limit, then opens and discharges. One is a control, the other is a safety device, and neither substitutes for the other — a building that needs a regulator generally needs both.

Most plumbing codes call for a regulator wherever static supply pressure at the building exceeds 80 psi. Past that point pressure stops being free performance and starts being wear: it is what splits supply lines, cuts fill valve seals and turns a dripping faucet into a replaced cartridge. Measure the street pressure with a gauge before choosing a set point rather than working from the neighborhood's reputation.

Installing a regulator closes the system, and a closed system needs somewhere for hot water to expand. Before the regulator, thermal expansion from the water heater pushed back out into the street main. After it, the regulator blocks that path, pressure climbs against nothing every time the burner fires, and the heater's T&P valve begins to weep — which reads as a failed T&P valve and is not one. The answer is a correctly sized thermal expansion tank put in at the same time, not a second T&P valve.

Adjustment range is a specification, not a preference. The standard range here is 25–75 psi and covers nearly every residential service. Low range valves adjust 10–35 psi and are stocked in 1/2" and 3/4" for services that have to land below what the standard valve will hold. Winding a 25–75 psi valve down to its bottom stop is not the same thing as fitting a low range valve.

Single union against double union is a serviceability decision rather than a hydraulic one. A single union valve is solid on one end, so replacing it later means cutting pipe. A double union breaks loose at both ends and the next valve goes in without touching the piping. On a service entrance buried behind finished wall, the double union is the cheaper part measured across the life of the building.

Ends cover the whole range — female NPT, solder union, press, PEX-A cold expansion and push-to-connect. The connection is a separate choice from the valve. The Resideo DS05, the DS06 DialSet and the Cash Acme EB45 are each stocked in several end configurations of one valve body, so choose the body for the pressure job and the ends for the pipe you are joining. Where Watts states the seat, it tracks size: polymer seat in 1/2" through 1", stainless steel seat in 1-1/4" through 2". The six Caleffi PressCal valves are listed to ASSE 1003 and carry an integral pressure gauge, in NPT and in press, 3/4" through 1-1/4".

Rebuild before replacing. Six of the 70 are service parts rather than valves: Resideo union kits for the DS06 and FK06 in 3/4", 1" and 1-1/2" NPT plus 3/4" sweat, a low lead replacement filter bowl with O-ring for the 1-1/2" and 2", and a union seal washer for the 1". A regulator that will not hold its setting is often a fouled strainer or a cut seal rather than a failed body — the DS06 carries its strainer in a replaceable bowl for that reason.

Body HTML:
60 backflow prevention devices from Watts, Zurn Wilkins, Apollo-Conbraco, Arrowhead Brass, Caleffi North America, Cash Acme, Aalberts Integrated Piping and Moen. Assemblies run 1/4" through 3"; air gap fittings cover 1/2" through 6". Most of the range is lead free bronze or lead free brass.

The device class is set by the hazard, not by the pipe size. A reduced pressure principle assembly — the RP, or RPZ where it is built as a reduced pressure zone assembly — is what a high hazard connection needs: it has a relief port that dumps to atmosphere the moment either check fouls, so a failure is visible on the floor instead of silent in the potable line. A double check assembly is a low hazard device and fails closed without telling anyone. A pressure vacuum breaker (PVB) protects against back-siphonage only, not back-pressure, which is why it belongs on irrigation and not on a boiler fill. Substituting down a class because it fits the budget is the one substitution that is never a field call.

On a lawn irrigation or sprinkler system the local code decides between a PVB and an RPZ backflow preventer, and the answer usually turns on whether fertilizer or chemical is injected downstream. A hose bib backflow preventer — a hose connection vacuum breaker threaded onto the sillcock — is the cheapest protection in the building and the one most often missing; eight are stocked here, four of them Watts in 3/4". A residential service entrance is typically a dual check, stocked from 1/4" through 1".

27 of the 60 are testable assemblies. Every reduced pressure, reduced pressure zone and double check assembly here carries test cocks, and in most jurisdictions has to be certified by a licensed tester at installation and then annually. That annual obligation follows the building, so specifying a testable assembly where the code does not require one commits the owner to a recurring cost.

Where the manufacturer publishes limits, the devices are rated 175 psi maximum working pressure and 180°F maximum temperature. ASSE 1013 covers reduced pressure principle assemblies and ASSE 1015 covers double checks; the number on the tag is what the inspector reads.

Rebuilding beats replacing on these. Eight Zurn Wilkins backflow preventer repair kits cover the 375, 375XL, 950XL, 975XL and 975XL2 from 1/4" through 2" — rubber and spring kits for an annual test failure, complete internals when the seats are cut. Match the kit to the model number on the tag, not to the pipe size.

The range breaks down as: reduced pressure principle (RP) assemblies (14), hose connection vacuum breakers (8), repair kits and internals (8), reduced pressure zone (RPZ) assemblies (7), double check valve assemblies (6), dual check valves (6), atmospheric and anti-siphon vacuum breakers (5), air gap fittings (4), pressure vacuum breaker (1), and a 2" Cash Acme EB45-U.

Swing, spring and dual check valves for potable water, hydronic heating and pump discharge, in 1/2" through 2" and larger.

Orientation is the specification people get wrong. A swing check relies on gravity and flow to close its disc, so it only works reliably in a horizontal run or a vertical run with upward flow — installed backwards or on a downflow line, it will not seat. A spring check closes against a spring and works in any orientation, which is why it is the right choice on pump discharge and in tight mechanical rooms.

Spring checks have a higher cracking pressure and therefore a higher pressure drop. On a gravity or low-head system that difference is enough to matter; on a pumped line it usually is not.

Shower and tub diverter valves, in-wall rough-in bodies and diverter trims, mostly 1/2" inlet.

A diverter sends water from one outlet to another — tub spout to showerhead, or between multiple shower outlets. A transfer valve is the related but different device: it can feed two outlets at once, which is what a body-spray and rain-head combination needs. Choosing a diverter where a transfer valve was intended means only one outlet ever runs.

Count outlets before ordering. Three-way and six-way diverters exist, and the number is fixed by the valve body in the wall, not by the trim on the face of it. Adding an outlet later means opening the wall.

Rough-in body and finish trim are ordered separately on most manufacturers' systems, which is what lets the valve go in during construction and the finish be chosen at the end. They must be from the same family — trim is not cross-compatible between brands or between generations.

Brands include Moen (M-CORE transfer valves and Posi-Temp with diverter), Grohe, hansgrohe, Delta, Brizo, American Standard, Pfister, TOTO and DXV, with 2-way, 3-way and 3-or-6-function diverter and transfer valve roughs.

The mixing valve that feeds the diverter is in shower and tub-shower valves; the finish trim is in shower trim sets and thermostatic valve trims.

Frequently asked questions

What does a shower diverter valve do?

A shower diverter valve sends water from the mixing valve to one outlet or another, such as the showerhead, a hand shower or a tub spout. The mixing valve sets the temperature; the diverter only chooses where the water goes.

What is a 3-way diverter valve?

A 3-way diverter has three outlet positions, so it can switch between three outlets, for example a showerhead, a hand shower and body sprays. Some 3-way diverters also have shared positions that run two outlets at once; check the product page.

Can I use a different brand of trim on my diverter valve?

No. The trim has to be made for the rough-in valve in the wall, so match the brand and model of the valve body. The rough-in and the trim are sold separately.

Diverter valve vs transfer valve: what is the difference?

A diverter valve sends all the water to one outlet at a time, such as the tub spout or the showerhead. A transfer valve can also run two outlets together, for example a rain head and body sprays. If you want two outlets on at the same time, choose a transfer valve or a diverter with shared positions.

2-way or 3-way diverter: which do I need?

Count the outlets. A 2-way diverter switches between two outlets, such as a showerhead and a hand shower. A 3-way diverter handles three, such as a showerhead, a hand shower and body sprays. The number is set by the rough-in body in the wall, so plan every outlet before the wall is closed.

How do I pick the right diverter valve?

Start with the brand and family of your mixing valve and trim, because trim only fits its own rough-in. Then match the number of outlets, the inlet connection (sweat, IPS or PEX) and the inlet size, which is 1/2" on most models here. The matching finish pieces are in diverter valve trims.

Ninety-two angle stops and straight stops - the small shut off valve under every sink and toilet - from BrassCraft (38), Legend Valve (28), Dahl Valve (19), LSP Products (4), Grohe (2) and BK Products (1). By body: 44 angle, 22 straight and 22 dual-outlet or tee, plus 4 kits and service stops.

Angle or straight is decided by the wall, not by preference

An angle stop turns the flow 90 degrees, so it is what you use when the supply pipe comes out of the wall and the fixture is above it. A straight stop passes flow in line, for when the pipe comes up out of the floor. That is the whole distinction, and it is the single most common ordering mistake on this category - the valve is otherwise identical inside. Look at the stub-out before you buy, not at the fixture.

The inlet is the decision. The outlet almost never is

Nearly every one of these ends in 3/8" or 1/4" compression on the fixture side, because that is what a supply line expects. The inlet is where the choice lives, and it has to match the pipe already in the wall:

  • Compression - 43 of them, for copper stub-outs
  • FIP - 17, threaded onto a male adapter or nipple
  • F1960 expansion PEX - 11, cold-expansion PEX-a
  • F1807 crimp PEX - 5, copper crimp ring PEX-b
  • Push-fit - 8, including Legend's Insta-Loc II
  • Press - 3 LegendPress, for a press tool
  • CPVC - 2, solvent weld

If you are on PEX, the inlet has to match your system: see F1960 expansion fittings and F1807 crimp fittings for which one you have.

Quarter-turn versus multi-turn

A quarter-turn stop is a ball valve - a chrome ball with a hole through it, sealed by two PTFE seats. A multi-turn stop is a compression washer on a rising stem. The difference matters after ten years, not on day one: the multi-turn washer hardens, bonds to the seat, and shears off when someone finally tries to close it during a leak. That is why a plumber replacing a faucet replaces the stop too. Twenty-nine of these are explicitly 1/4-turn ball type; the Legend 114-201NL is the one deliberate multi-turn in the range.

A compression ferrule is single-use

The brass ring that seals a compression inlet deforms permanently when you tighten the nut. It has taken the shape of that pipe at that depth. Pull the valve off and reuse the old ferrule and it will weep - not immediately, which is worse. Cut the stub back and start with a new ferrule, or use a push-fit or press inlet where the seal is a captured O-ring rather than a crushed ring.

Push-fit and press inlets

Eight push-fit stops, including Legend's Insta-Loc II (114-903NL, 114-904NL, 114-943NL) and BrassCraft's G2PS and G2QPS series, go on a clean cut stub with no tool at all. Three LegendPress stops (114-903PNL, 114-904PNL, 114-913PNL) take a standard press jaw - see press tools and jaws. Both cost more per valve than compression and both pay for themselves the moment you are working in a cabinet you cannot get two wrenches into.

Dual stops and tees

Twenty-two dual-outlet stops and tees, for one stub-out feeding two things: a toilet plus a bidet seat, a sink plus a reverse-osmosis unit, a dishwasher teed off the hot side. BrassCraft's CR1900DVX and R1700DVX families and Legend's 114-801NL and 114-802NL give two independently controlled outlets, usually 3/8" and 1/4". The BrassCraft CT2-664X P and BK 993-016NL are plain tees with no second valve - cheaper, but you lose the ability to shut one branch without the other.

Loose key stops

The BrassCraft KTSCR19X and SCR19X have no handle. They take a removable key, which is what you want in a rental, a school restroom or anywhere a handle would get turned by someone who should not be turning it. Order the key separately and keep it on the truck.

No-lead is not a marketing line

Legend's "No Lead" and LSP's "Lead Free" markings refer to the federal limit that has applied to every potable-water valve sold in the US since 2014: a weighted average of no more than 0.25 percent lead on wetted surfaces, certified to NSF/ANSI 372. Older rough-brass stops from before that rule are still in millions of houses. If you are replacing one on a potable line, the new one has to be certified.

Related

A stop is half of a pair - the supply lines that thread onto it are on their own page. For what sits at the other end, see toilet tanks, toilet repair parts, centerset faucets and pull-out kitchen faucets, or the full bathroom department.

Not sure which of the three you need? Our whole-house water leak detection guide covers valve sizing, where each device installs, what each tier costs and how the sensors are wired.

Whole-house shut-off valves go on the main downstream of the service shutoff and close the entire supply when a sensor trips. The Resideo L5 is an actuator on a lead-free ball valve, shipped with a power adapter, a mounting clip and a 5 ft sensing cable, in 1/2", 3/4", 1" and 1-1/4" NPT. Size the valve to the line you are cutting into, not to a fixture branch: a 1" main needs a 1" valve or the whole house loses pressure through the device.

Appliance shut-off kits cover the known failure points for a fraction of the price of a whole-house valve. FloodStop builds one kit per appliance: 3/4" NPT MIP x FIP for a water heater, two 3/4" 90-degree valves for a washing machine, 1/4" compression for an ice maker and 3/8" compression for a toilet or dishwasher. Taco's LeakBreaker is water-heater specific, a control unit with valve, actuator and sensor that shuts the supply to the heater, with a two-color LED and an audible alarm. It is re-settable and testable after a trip, and the eLink version reports status over WiFi.

Point sensors raise the alarm but close nothing. The Resideo L1 detects water on its own base or anywhere along its 5 ft sensing cable, runs on WiFi with no hub, sounds a 100 dB alarm and sends an app notification. It also reads temperature and humidity, so it warns before a pipe freezes rather than after it bursts. Battery life runs up to three years, the unit is reusable once wiped dry, and cables daisy-chain to cover up to 500 feet from a single detector.

Frequently asked questions

Whole-house shut-off or appliance shut-off?

A whole-house valve installs on the main water line and can shut off the entire home when any sensor detects a leak. An appliance shut-off protects one point, such as a water heater, washing machine or ice maker, and costs less to install.

Do water leak detectors need Wi-Fi?

Wi-Fi models send alerts to your phone and can close a valve remotely. Battery-only detectors sound a local alarm, which helps only if someone is home to hear it.

What size shut-off valve do I need?

Match the size of the main water line where the valve will be installed. Valves are offered from 1/2 in to 1-1/4 in NPT.

Thermostats and thermostat accessories from Resideo, tekmar Control Systems, Southwire and DiversiTech. Resideo is the company that builds and sells the Honeywell Home line, so a thermostat listed by its Resideo number, such as TH6220WF, is the one sold at retail as the Honeywell Home T6 Pro — same part, two names. Families stocked here: PRO 1000, PRO 2000, PRO 3000 and CommercialPRO 7000; the T-series from T1 Pro through T10 Pro; FocusPRO 5000 and 6000; VisionPRO 8000; WiFi 9000; and Prestige IAQ.

Voltage decides the thermostat before anything else does. A low-voltage thermostat runs on 24V through the equipment transformer and is what gas furnaces, heat pumps, boilers and air handlers use. A line-voltage thermostat switches 120V or 240V directly and is for electric baseboard, electric radiant panels and fan-forced wall heaters. They are not interchangeable. Wiring a 24V thermostat to a 240V baseboard circuit is a fire risk, not a malfunction, and the mistake is easy to make because the two look alike on the wall.

Line voltage thermostats are stocked for electric heat, single-pole and double-pole, manual and 7-day programmable. Single-pole leaves one leg energized when the dial is off; double-pole breaks both. If the heater has to be fully dead at the thermostat, it has to be double-pole.

Millivolt is the third case and it catches people out. A standing-pilot wall heater or gas fireplace generates its own 750 mV from the thermopile and has no transformer at all; it needs a millivolt-rated thermostat, and a digital 24V unit will simply not close the circuit. Heat-only millivolt models are stocked for exactly this.

The C-wire is the most common reason a Wi-Fi thermostat replacement stalls. Older homes were wired with four conductors and no common, and a smart thermostat needs continuous 24V to run its display and radio. Either pull new cable or add an adapter — the Resideo WireSaver THP9045A1023 puts the common back at the equipment end without opening walls.

Resideo splits connected control two ways and they solve different problems. Wi-Fi models talk to the house router and the phone app: T6 Pro Smart, the Wi-Fi VisionPRO 8000, and the WiFi 9000 color touchscreen. RedLINK is Resideo’s own 900 MHz link between the thermostat and its own accessories — wireless indoor and outdoor sensors, equipment interface modules, remote modules and the TrueZONE adapter — and it works where there is no reliable Wi-Fi at the equipment. RedLINK modules and sensors are in RedLINK accessories. The T10 Pro and Prestige IAQ kits use both.

Southwire thermostat wire is stocked in 18/2, 18/4, 18/5 and 18/6, in 250 ft and 500 ft. Count the conductors against the system before ordering: a straight heat-cool job lives on four, a heat pump with auxiliary heat and a common wants six, and pulling the smaller roll is how a job ends up needing a C-wire adapter later.

Frequently asked questions

Are Honeywell Home and Resideo thermostats the same?

Yes. Resideo builds and supports the Honeywell Home line, so a Resideo part number such as TH6220WF is the same thermostat sold at retail as the Honeywell Home T6 Pro.

Do I need a low-voltage or a line-voltage thermostat?

Gas furnaces, heat pumps, boilers and air handlers use a low-voltage (24V) thermostat. Electric baseboard, convector and radiant floor heat use a line voltage thermostat rated for 120V or 240V. If the old thermostat is connected with heavy wires and wire nuts, it is almost certainly line voltage.

Do I need a C-wire for a Wi-Fi thermostat?

Most Wi-Fi thermostats need continuous 24V power from a common (C) wire. If the wall has no C-wire, a C-wire adapter such as the Resideo THP9045A1023 WireSaver adds one at the equipment without pulling new cable.

Non-programmable thermostats for forced air and hydronic heating — a fixed setpoint you turn, with no schedule to configure.

They exist because a schedule is a liability in some installations, not a feature. A rental unit, a commercial space with irregular hours, a garage, a workshop or a tenant who will fight the programming all work better with a thermostat that holds one temperature until someone changes it. They also have far fewer service calls, because there is nothing to reprogram after a power outage and no battery to die.

Match the stage count to the equipment: a single-stage furnace, a two-stage furnace and a heat pump with auxiliary heat all need different terminal configurations, and a thermostat with too few stages will run the equipment but never use its second stage. Heat pumps specifically need a thermostat that supports reversing valve and emergency heat.

These are low-voltage (24V) controls. Electric baseboard and radiant panels need line-voltage thermostats instead, which switch 120V or 240V directly — the two are not interchangeable.

Predominantly Honeywell Home by Resideo, with DiversiTech. Families include the PRO 1000, T1 Pro, T3 Pro, PRO 3000, FocusPRO 5000 and the mechanical T87, T822 and T834. See also: Honeywell Pro Series thermostats, programmable thermostats, line voltage thermostats and thermostat accessories.

Frequently asked questions

What is a non-programmable thermostat?

It holds one setpoint until someone changes it, with no schedule to configure. That makes it a good fit for rentals, commercial spaces with irregular hours, garages and workshops.

Will a non-programmable thermostat work with my heat pump?

Only if the model is rated for heat pumps. Check that it supports the reversing valve (O/B) and auxiliary or emergency heat, and that its heat and cool stages match the equipment.

Do these thermostats need batteries or a C-wire?

Many Honeywell Home PRO and FocusPRO models can run on AA batteries or on 24V from a common (C) wire. Check the power options on the product page before installing.

What is the difference between a heat-only and a heat/cool thermostat?

A heat-only thermostat controls a furnace, boiler or other heating appliance and has no cooling terminal. A heat/cool thermostat also switches an air conditioner or heat pump. Honeywell heat-only models here include the T87K1007/U, the T822K1000/U and the PRO 1000 TH1100DV1000/U. For a system with central air, choose a heat/cool model such as the PRO 3000 TH3110D1008/U or the FocusPRO 5000 TH5110D1022/U.

Battery or C-wire: which do I need?

Mechanical models such as the T87 and T822 need neither batteries nor a C-wire. Digital models need power for the display: battery-powered models run on AA batteries, so they work where there is no common (C) wire, while a C-wire supplies 24V continuously, so there are no batteries to replace. If the old thermostat has no C-wire, choose a model that can run on batteries.

The setback is where the savings come from, and it works differently on different equipment. A furnace recovers quickly, so a deep overnight setback pays. A heat pump does not — a large setback forces the auxiliary resistance heat to make up the difference on recovery, which costs more than the setback saved. Heat pump installations need a thermostat with adaptive or intelligent recovery, and a shallow setback.

Stage count has to match the equipment. A two-stage furnace on a single-stage thermostat runs on high fire only and loses both the efficiency and the comfort the second stage was bought for. Check the terminal designations against the appliance wiring, not against the old thermostat — the old one may itself have been wrong.

C-wire is the practical obstacle on retrofit. Many older installations have no common wire, and a thermostat that needs continuous power will short-cycle or fail without one.

Which schedule type do I need?

A 5-2 schedule uses one program for weekdays and one for the weekend, a 5-1-1 schedule adds separate Saturday and Sunday programs, and a 7-day schedule sets every day on its own.

Is a programmable thermostat a good idea with a heat pump?

Yes, with a heat pump-rated model and a shallow setback. A large setback makes the auxiliary heat run during recovery, which can cost more than the setback saves.

Do programmable thermostats need a C-wire?

Many PRO and FocusPRO models can run on batteries, but models with backlit or touchscreen displays usually need 24V from a common (C) wire. Check the power options on the product page.

Which Honeywell programmable thermostat works with a heat pump?

Line-voltage thermostats switch electric baseboard, convector and floor heating directly at 120 or 240 V, with no transformer or relay in between.

Check the thermostat's current rating against the heater load (many models carry 16.7 A). Double-pole models disconnect both legs of a 240 V circuit and give a true off position; single-pole models break one leg only.

For electric floor heating, use a floor-heating thermostat with a floor sensor. GA models include a 5 mA GFCI, which floor heating installations typically require. Mechanical baseboard thermostats (T498) and programmable electronic models (TL8130, TL8230, TH106, TH115) are both stocked.

Frequently asked questions

What is a line voltage thermostat?

It switches a 120V or 240V electric heater directly, with no transformer or relay. It is used for electric baseboard, convectors, fan-forced wall heaters and radiant floor heat, and it is not interchangeable with a 24V thermostat.

Single-pole or double-pole?

A double-pole thermostat breaks both legs of a 240V circuit and has a true off position. A single-pole model breaks one leg only, so the heater stays connected to power even when it is off.

How do I size a baseboard heater thermostat?

Add up the wattage of the heaters on the circuit and check it against the thermostat's current rating at your voltage. Many models are rated 16.7 A, which is about 4,000 W at 240V.

Is there a smart or wireless option for electric baseboard heat?

Yes. The Honeywell Home TLM1110R1000 and Aube ATM100-SPK are RedLINK wireless line voltage equipment interface modules for electric baseboard, convectors and fan-forced heaters at 100-240V. They are listed in RedLINK accessories. Pair them with a compatible RedLINK thermostat.

Which cover plate fits my thermostat?

What is the difference between the PRO and T Pro series?

Honeywell Home TrueZONE dampers split one forced-air system into zones, each controlled by its own thermostat.

Rectangular parallel blade dampers (ZD series) are sized to the duct, width by height in inches, from 6 x 6 in upward. Order the damper to the inside duct dimension so it fits without transitions. Each damper connects to a TrueZONE zone panel, which opens and closes the dampers on each thermostat's call.

When only one small zone calls, the blower is still moving air for the whole house. A bypass damper relieves that excess static pressure, and it is sized with the zone dampers, not after.

Frequently asked questions

How do I size a rectangular zone damper?

Measure the inside width and height of the duct and order that size. For example, a ZD10X16TZ fits a 10 x 16 in duct.

Do I need a bypass damper?

Often, yes. When a small zone calls on its own, the blower still moves air for the whole house, and a bypass damper relieves that extra static pressure. Size it together with the zone dampers.

Can I replace just the damper motor?

Yes. The Honeywell Home M847D-ZONE replacement motor fits ARD and ZD dampers, so a failed motor can be swapped without cutting the damper out of the duct.

Whole-house humidifiers, dehumidifiers, steam humidifiers and the humidifier replacement parts that keep them running, all from Honeywell Home (Resideo).

The three humidifier types differ in how they get water into the air. Bypass units, such as the TrueEASE HE100, HE150, HE200 and HE250, use furnace airflow across an evaporator pad and need a bypass duct. Fan-powered units like the HE300 and HE365 carry their own blower and need no bypass. Steam units such as the HM750 electrode humidifier boil water and add moisture whether or not the furnace is running; parts for the HM700, HM750 and TrueSTEAM are stocked.

The evaporator pad is a consumable. It scales up with minerals and stops absorbing, which shows up as a humidifier that runs but delivers nothing; annual replacement is normal maintenance. Most of this collection is OEM parts listed by the models they fit: HC22 and HC26 pads, solenoid valves, circuit boards, distribution trays, electrode cylinders and dehumidifier filters for the DR65, DR90 and DR120. Match the part to the model number on the unit's label.

Control placement decides whether the system behaves: a wall control such as the HumidiPRO H6062 reads the living space, which is what the occupant actually feels.

Body HTML:
Whole-house air cleaners, media filters, filter cabinets, conversion kits and replacement parts from Resideo.

A media air cleaner is a four- to five-inch deep cabinet holding a pleated filter, and the depth is the whole advantage. The extra surface area captures finer particles at a lower pressure drop than a one-inch throwaway, and it lasts six to twelve months instead of thirty days.

Pressure drop is the specification most often ignored. A high-MERV filter in a system not designed for it starves the blower, which shows up as reduced airflow, longer run times and, on a furnace, high-limit trips. MERV 11 to 13 is the usual practical ceiling for residential equipment; higher belongs with a blower sized for it.

Retrofitting a media cabinet needs physical space at the return plenum, and that constraint decides most jobs before filter choice does.

Electronic air cleaners work differently — they charge particles and collect them on plates that are washed rather than replaced, so the running cost is labor instead of filters.

Popular part numbers: Honeywell FC100A1037, Honeywell POPUP2020, Honeywell F100F2020, Honeywell FC37A1130, Honeywell UV2400U1000.

Frequently asked questions

Which replacement filter fits my cabinet?

Match the part number printed on the old filter or the cabinet model (for example F100 or F200) and the face size. Media filters are sized to the cabinet, not to the duct.

How often should a media filter be replaced?

Follow the cabinet manual. Deep media filters last longer than 1 in filters, but replace them sooner if airflow drops or the filter looks loaded.

Do you carry electronic air cleaner parts?

Yes: replacement cells, prefilters, postfilters, power supplies and ionizer wires, all matched by part number. See all Honeywell Home parts.

Resideo combination gas valves for furnaces, boilers and water heaters, matched to the appliance's ignition system.

Choose by ignition type first. Standing pilot valves (VR8200) keep a pilot lit at all times; intermittent pilot valves (VR8204, VR8304) light the pilot on each call for heat; direct ignition valves (VR8205, VR8305) light the main burner with a hot surface or spark igniter and no pilot. The ignition control and the valve have to match.

Then check inlet and outlet size (1/2 x 1/2 in or 3/4 x 3/4 in), opening characteristic (standard, slow or step opening), single or two-stage, and the regulator setting for the fuel. Many models ship set for natural gas with an LP conversion kit available.

Water heater gas valves (WT8840, WT8860) are listed by the tank brand they replace, including Rheem, A.O. Smith and Bradford White.

Frequently asked questions

How do I find the right replacement gas valve?

Read the model number printed on the old valve, for example VR8205Q2555 or VR8305M3506, and order the same number. If it is no longer made, match the ignition type, the inlet and outlet size, the opening type and the number of stages.

Can a natural gas valve be converted to LP?

Many VR8200 and VR8300 series valves accept a regulator conversion kit, such as the 393691 LP kit or the 394588 natural gas kit. Conversions should be done by a qualified gas technician.

Are Honeywell and Resideo gas valves the same?

Yes. Resideo makes the former Honeywell gas valve line, and the part numbers did not change. See all Resideo controls.

Frequently asked questions

What is a switching relay used for?

It lets a 24V thermostat or control switch a line voltage load such as a circulator pump, fan or burner.

Which relay do I need for a baseboard or duct heater?

Use an electric heat relay such as the RC840 or R841. Models with a T suffix include a built-in transformer, so they supply their own 24V control power.

How do I match a replacement relay?

Match the coil voltage and the contact arrangement (SPST, SPDT or DPST) and check the contact rating against the load you are switching.

Thermostats, gas valves, ignition assemblies and components, aquastats and wells, zone valves and actuators, pressure relief valves, switching relays, transformers, fan and limit controllers, sensors and low water cut-offs.

Most of what is here is a replacement part, and Resideo parts are model-specific. Gas valves and ignition assemblies in particular are matched to the appliance and often to a serial range within one model, because the manufacturer revises the component without changing the appliance name. Two things that decide the right part. Voltage: low-voltage (24V) controls drive a system through a transformer and relay and cover most gas and hydronic equipment, while line-voltage switches 120V or 240V directly and belongs to electric baseboard and radiant — connecting one to the wrong system is a fire risk, not a malfunction. And an aquastat has to be paired with the correct immersion well, seated to the bottom with conducting paste, or it reads the air in the well and responds late.

Working from an older Honeywell part number? The model numbering carried over when Resideo was spun off in 2018, so a number from an old manual will usually identify a current part. Frequently asked questions

Is Resideo the same company as Honeywell Home?

Resideo was spun off from Honeywell in 2018 and makes and supports the Honeywell Home product line. Many part numbers are sold under both names, so an older Honeywell number usually identifies a current Resideo part.

Which thermostat do I need for electric baseboard heat?

Electric baseboard and radiant heaters need a line voltage thermostat that switches 120V or 240V directly, such as the T498 series. A 24V low-voltage thermostat cannot be connected to a baseboard circuit. See line voltage thermostats.

What does a manual reset limit control do?

A limit control shuts the burner off when the temperature at its sensor reaches the limit setting. A manual reset model stays off until someone presses the reset button, so the cause of the overheat gets checked first. See fan and limit controllers.
